cards.title: 厄尔尼诺加剧印尼野火，婆罗洲红毛猩猩救援行动紧张进行

entities.name: 厄尔尼诺
entities.explain: 一种自然气候现象，会导致太平洋东部海水异常变暖，常引发全球多地干旱或暴雨等极端天气。

entities.name: 红毛猩猩
entities.explain: 一种珍稀的大型灵长类动物，主要生活在东南亚的雨林中，以树栖生活为主，目前濒临灭绝。

entities.name: YIARI
entities.explain: 印度尼西亚国际动物救援基金会，一个在婆罗洲从事野生动物救援和保护的非政府组织。

cards.summary: 随着厄尔尼诺现象加强，印尼多地野火蔓延，婆罗洲的救援人员正努力营救越来越多的红毛猩猩。据YIARI组织称，截至8月已成功救出7只。火灾正摧毁它们的栖息地，救援行动面临严峻挑战。
cards.relevant: 红毛猩猩是极度濒危物种，野火对其种群生存构成直接威胁，也反映了气候变化背景下生物多样性保护的紧迫性。
cards.context: 厄尔尼诺现象通常会导致印尼地区干旱少雨，极易引发森林火灾。这些火灾不仅破坏生态环境，也直接威胁到包括红毛猩猩在内的野生动物的生存。

cards.title: 科学家启动开创性项目，研究阿拉斯加北极生态系统能否整体适应气候危机

entities.name: 北极生态系统
entities.explain: 指北极地区包括冻原、河流、动植物等在内的整个自然环境系统，对气候变化极为敏感。

entities.name: 白冠麻雀
entities.explain: 一种在北极地区繁殖的候鸟，夏季从南方迁徙至此，以昆虫为食。

entities.name: 布鲁克斯山脉
entities.explain: 位于阿拉斯加北部的一条山脉，是北极地区的重要地理标志。

cards.summary: 在阿拉斯加北坡，科学家们正开展一项前所未有的研究，探索整个北极生态系统（包括溪流和冻原）是否能通过物种间的协同适应来应对气候变化，而非仅依赖单物种的优胜劣汰。他们通过捕捉白冠麻雀并采集样本，研究其食物来源的变化。
cards.relevant: 该研究可能改变人们对物种适应气候变化的传统认知，为生态保护提供新的科学依据。
cards.context: 气候变化对北极地区影响尤为剧烈，冻土融化、物种迁徙模式改变等问题日益严重。传统观点认为物种需独立适应，但此项目首次从生态系统整体角度研究适应机制。
cards.source_analysis: 《卫报》是英国主流媒体，其环境报道通常具有较高的科学严谨性，立场偏向关注气候变化议题。
cards.social_impact: 研究结果可能为全球生态保护政策提供参考，尤其是在如何帮助生态系统整体应对气候变化方面。
cards.source_text: On Alaska’s North Slope, scientists tread carefully across clumps of tussock grasses toward a fast-flowing stream draining the imposing Brooks Range of ice and snow. Near Galbraith Creek, they string out a mist net for white-crowned sparrows. The birds have recently arrived from southerly latitudes, intent on feasting on the insects that will soon descend on the tundra like storm clouds. The Arctic summer is short-lived, and sparrows have only a few weeks to establish territories, find mates, lay eggs and raise their chicks on a steady diet of bugs. From every ensnared bird, the scientists collect blood, feather and faecal samples to see what they are eating and how that changes over the summer. One thing they want to know is whether the sparrows are consuming a lot of stream insects, such as stoneflies and mayflies, says Ian Shuman, a doctoral student in quantitative ecology at Columbia University. As willow shrubs claim new territory along the Arctic’s rivers and streams – a process scientists call “shrubification” – this could disrupt the life cycles of stoneflies and mayflies. If the songbirds also depend on aquatic insects to thrive, that might affect the sparrows’ prospects. The tundra can feel immutable in its vastness. A sea of grass and moss extends as far as the eye can see. But above the Arctic Circle, change is happening faster than anywhere else on Earth. Snow is melting earlier in the spring, sending torrents of water downstream. By late summer, such early season deluges have given way to parched creek beds. The Arctic grayling – cold water fish in the salmon family – that swim between deep lake winter refuges and shallow summer spawning streams may become stranded in isolated pools. Their survival, too, rests on the mayflies and stoneflies. Across the planet, global heating is reshuffling the order of life. Some species will prosper, while those that can’t adapt quickly enough will nosedive toward extinction. Evolution and adaptation have long been thought of as solitary endeavours – a survival of the fittest. But what if species could instead draw on their longstanding relationships not to succeed or fail alone, but to swiftly evolve and adapt together to climate breakdown, keeping whole ecosystems intact? cards.title: 美国人文专业学士学位授予数量降至30多年来最低点

entities.name: 人文专业
entities.explain: 指文学、历史、哲学、语言学等研究人类文化和思想的学科。

entities.name: 美国艺术与科学院
entities.explain: 美国一个历史悠久的荣誉学会和独立政策研究中心，其人文指标项目提供相关数据。

cards.summary: 根据美国艺术与科学院人文指标项目的最新报告，2025年美国高校授予的人文学士学位数量仅为164,847个，是自1991年以来的最低点，比2012年的高峰下降了30.4%。几乎所有人文子学科的学位授予数量都在下降，其中宗教学降幅最大。
cards.relevant: 人文学科持续遇冷反映了就业市场导向、教育成本上升及社会对理工科偏好的变化，可能影响未来社会的人文素养和批判性思维。
cards.context: 过去二十年，美国大学人文学科入学率持续下滑，学生和家长更倾向于选择就业前景更明确的STEM（科学、技术、工程、数学）领域。
cards.source_analysis: Daily Nous是一个哲学领域的新闻网站，其报道可能带有对人文学科价值的关切立场。
cards.social_impact: 数据显示2021至2023年间人文学位数量急剧下降12.7%，但2023年后降幅趋缓，2024至2025年仅下降0.4%，可能预示着下降趋势正在触底。
cards.source_text: Fewer and Fewer Students Earn Degrees in the Humanities。20 years ago, nearly 15% of the undergraduate degrees conferred in the United States were in the humanities. As of 2025, that percentage is down to 8.1%. These figures are from a recent report by Humanities Indicators, a project of the American Academy of Arts & Sciences. Here are the numbers: In 2025, the nation’s colleges and universities awarded 164,847 bachelor’s degrees in the humanities—the smallest number of degrees awarded since 1991 and 30.4% below the recent high-water mark in 2012… That decline includes a particularly sharp drop of 12.7% from 2021 to 2023, followed by a more modest drop of 2.1% from 2023 to 2024, and a further decline of just 0.4% from 2024 to 2025—the smallest year-on-year decline since 2012. And most disciplines within the humanities have shown a decline: Within the humanities, almost every discipline awarded fewer degrees in 2025 than 13 years earlier… The largest proportional drops in degrees awarded occurred in religious studies (down 56.3%), area studies (53.2%), languages and literatures other than English (50.8%), English (43.8%), history (40.6%), classical studies (39.4%), and comparative literature (31%). Only three disciplines showed increases—folklore (where the small number of degrees awarded makes the numbers highly volatile), the study of the arts (with a modest 2.1% increase since 2012), and interdisciplinary humanities disciplines (where the increase was largely due to the addition of a substantial number of new programs, such as digital humanities, in the Department of Education’s 2020 revision of its Classification of Instructional Programs). How’s philosophy doing? Well, after a slight decrease last year, there has been a slight increase: In 2024, 5,763 students earned philosophy BAs. In 2025, that number was 5,918. The full report from Humanities Indicators is here. The post Fewer and Fewer Students Earn Degrees in the Humanities first appeared on Daily Nous .

cards.title: 《我的孩子该做什么？》书评：呼吁拥抱AI教育机遇的乐观之作

entities.name: 丹尼尔·萨斯金德
entities.explain: 本书作者，一位关注科技与社会发展的学者。

entities.name: AI
entities.explain: 人工智能，指计算机系统模拟人类智能的技术，在教育领域可提供个性化学习等应用。

cards.summary: 《卫报》刊发书评，介绍丹尼尔·萨斯金德的新书《我的孩子该做什么？》。书评认为，这本书令人耳目一新地乐观，呼吁人们抓住人工智能在教育中的机遇，而不是因恐惧而退缩。书中以1979年计算器进入课堂时的争议为引，类比当下对AI的担忧。
cards.relevant: 在AI快速渗透各行各业的背景下，教育领域如何应对成为全球家长和教育者关注的焦点，本书提供了积极视角。
cards.context: 每当新技术出现，教育界常伴随恐慌。1979年计算器普及曾引发对算术能力下降的担忧，如今AI也面临类似争议。萨斯金德在书中主张积极拥抱而非抗拒。
cards.source_analysis: 《卫报》书籍评论版块，通常由专业书评人撰写，立场相对中立，注重文化评论。
cards.social_impact: 该书评可能引发关于AI在教育中角色的公共讨论，影响家长和教育政策制定者的态度。
cards.source_text: In 1979, the government asked Wilfred Cockcroft, a now largely forgotten maths lecturer from the University of Hull, to write a report about a crisis in the teaching of his subject to children. It was wide-ranging and meticulous, and included a chapter on a technological innovation that was suddenly becoming available to the average consumer: the calculator. Many parents and teachers feared that the gadget would undermine a basic skill and a pillar of education – one of the sacred three Rs – producing generations of dumbed-down drones who could reach for a device in their pockets to avoid the hard graft of arithmetic. But Cockcroft didn’t see it that way. Instead, he proposed embracing rather than fearing the calculator. Students should be taught with and without one – and tested accordingly. “Cockcroft is unwilling to pretend that the oncoming wave of technological progress can be dodged,” economist Daniel Susskind writes in his urgent new book. A former Downing Street policy wonk who is now also a researcher at the Institute for Ethics in AI at Oxford University, Susskind casts himself as the Cockroft of the 2020s. In an era of confusion and hand-wringing (if not outright panic) about the implications of AI, he makes the technologist’s case for breathing, learning and grasping the opportunities it presents. The maths comparison only goes so far, of course; even accounting for the hubris of the AI industry, its achievements have already wrought changes that now make the calculator seem about as consequential as the corkscrew. But while the scale of the disruption is new, the historical context is, to some extent, reassuring. The book’s title neatly taps into the techno-angst of the modern parent about a future of extreme uncertainty. If traditionally we passed down wisdom with an open-minded but fairly clear sense of how it might apply to a new generation, “today, it feels like that sense of continuity has broken. In truth, we cannot be sure the advice we gave our children last year still works for the next.” Susskind, a father of young children himself, tries to anticipate a future of artificial general intelligence (AGI) – when AI will outperform us at every economically useful task. (We now have access, via ChatGPT, Claude and the like, to what’s known as artificial narrow intelligence: systems that are good at performing specific tasks.) cards.title: 宇航员拍摄的地球新影像：展现人类日益增长的重要性而非渺小

entities.name: Artemis II
entities.explain: 美国宇航局（NASA）的载人登月任务，此次为绕月飞行，是自1972年以来首次有宇航员接近月球。

entities.name: 暗淡蓝点
entities.explain: 指1990年旅行者1号探测器在60亿公里外拍摄的地球照片，地球在其中只是一个微小光点，常被用来象征人类的渺小。

cards.summary: Aeon网站发布了一段来自2026年Artemis II绕月飞行任务中宇航员拍摄的地球影像。该视频被认为可能成为新时代的“暗淡蓝点”，但它揭示的不是人类的微不足道，而是我们日益增长的重要性。
cards.relevant: 该影像提供了一个全新的视角，促使人们反思人类在宇宙中的角色以及我们对地球的影响力。
cards.context: 1990年的“暗淡蓝点”照片强调了地球在宇宙中的渺小。而此次由宇航员在绕月飞行中拍摄的新影像，因技术更先进且视角不同，被赋予新的哲学意义。
cards.source_analysis: Aeon是一家专注于哲学、科学和社会议题的在线杂志，内容偏向深度思考和文化评论。
cards.social_impact: 该影像可能成为新的文化符号，激发公众对太空探索和人类处境的讨论。
cards.source_text: During the Artemis II crewed mission around the Moon in April 2026, the NASA astronaut Reid Wiseman took a series of photographs capturing the nightside of Earth illuminated by moonlight. After the photographs were released to the public, a Redditor combined several of them to create a dynamic image. In this video essay, the popular US YouTuber Hank Green makes the case that – like the famed ‘Earthrise’ photo, the ‘Pale Blue Dot’ image popularised by Carl Sagan, and the Hubble Deep Field pictures containing thousands of galaxies – watching this brief timelapse is an awe-inspiring experience, even if it doesn’t necessarily convey any new information. However, unlike those earlier images, its message isn’t one of our extraordinary smallness. Instead, with its dance of naturally occurring and human-made phenomena, the story it tells is one of our growing significance – for better and for worse. Image by Reid Wiseman/NASA. cards.context: Vantara动物园一直因其动物来源和福利问题受到批评。此次被曝与有狩猎背景的游说公司合作，加深了外界对其背后利益关系的质疑。

cards.title: 哥伦比亚原住民守护者面临压力，被迫适应“世界之心”地区的变迁

entities.name: Wiwa社区
entities.explain: 哥伦比亚一个原住民群体，世代居住于内华达山脉圣玛尔塔地区，视其为“世界之心”。

entities.name: 圣玛尔塔内华达山脉
entities.explain: 位于哥伦比亚北部的一座孤立山脉，生物多样性丰富，是多个原住民社区的圣地和家园。

cards.summary: 在哥伦比亚的圣玛尔塔内华达山脉，Wiwa社区的家庭正在低坡的干旱森林中建造新家园。他们的祖居地位于山上更高的茂密丛林，如今因各种压力，许多原住民社区正被迫迁移和适应。
cards.relevant: 该事件反映了全球原住民社区在环境变化和发展压力下，如何维护其文化传统和土地权利的普遍问题。
cards.context: 哥伦比亚的“世界之心”地区正面临气候变化、非法开采和发展项目等多重压力，迫使原住民社区离开祖居地，寻找新的生存方式。
cards.source_analysis: Mongabay的报道通常基于实地采访，关注环境正义和原住民权利，立场同情原住民。

cards.source_text: - Indigenous Wiwa families in Colombia’s Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta are moving farther downslope in an effort to preserve community cohesion amid climate and security pressures. - The mountain range’s Indigenous nations continue to hold to a “law of origin” that guides their path amid intensifying pressures from armed violence, resource extraction, and climate change. - Wiwa leaders describe sacred sites, rivers and forests as “living curricula,” inseparable from cultural and ecological responsibilities. - Recent protections have expanded the protected parts of the Sierra Nevada and prohibited new bids for mining and fossil fuel extraction. RIOHACHA, Colombia — Amid the low slopes of a tropical dry forest, families from the Wiwa community of Gomke are building a new home. Their ancestral settlement lies higher on a lush mountain in the town of Dibulla, overlooking the Caribbean coast in Colombia’s Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta. Across this region, many Indigenous communities have been forcibly displaced by climate-related disasters or uprooted by armed actors. Gomke’s move to lower terrain, however, is described by community representatives as voluntary: a collectively led adaptation strategy to protect social, educational and spiritual cohesion amid intensifying climate pressures and the presence of paramilitary groups. They call their new settlement Shegunamke. The Wiwa have also acquired other parcels of land elsewhere in the Sierra, including at higher elevations. “We have left [those] untouched so that rivers, springs and bodies of water do not die,” said Roberto Carlos Coronado Calvo, rector of Shenzhawimaku, the Wiwa educational institution that combines conventional learning with the community’s language, culture, knowledge systems and relationship to the territory. “If we begin clearing and cutting into the páramo [ecosystem], how can we guarantee life for those living below?” Across the Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta, known to its peoples as Gonawindúa, or the “Heart of the World,” the four Indigenous nations of Arhuaco, Kankuamo, Kogui and Wiwa are navigating deep changes driven by agro-industrial expansion, legal and illegal mining (driven by rising global gold prices), the return of paramilitary violence tied to the drug trade, and accelerating climate impacts within and around the Línea Negra, their ancestral network of sacred sites. cards.source_text: Few birds are quite as elegant as the blue crane. As I watched a pair feeding alongside a busy road in South Africa, against the rather incongruous backdrop of a herd of cows, I was struck by their sheer beauty. With a slender body, curved neck, long legs, elongated tail plumes and a subtle, dove-grey plumage, this bird really is the avian equivalent of a catwalk model. But not all is well for the blue crane. It has the smallest global range of any of the world’s 15 crane species: apart from an isolated population in Namibia, almost all are found in South Africa, where it is celebrated as the national bird. Once common and widespread, blue crane numbers have fallen steadily over the past 50 years, and today between only 25,000 and 46,000 individuals remain in the wild. If the downward trend continues, this species faces a genuine risk of extinction. The reasons for the decline are tediously predictable. As a grassland specialist, when intensive farming takes over, the food supply is inevitably reduced. A lethal cocktail of threats, including illegal poisoning, disturbance, habitat loss and the climate crisis – which this year brought unseasonably early rains followed by drought – mean that its future is far from rosy. But as I watched these beautiful birds, I could forget about their plight for a few moments and quietly rejoice in their exquisite grace.

cards.source_text: Frank Lloyd Wright was often strapped for cash. In that respect, he had something in common with Vincent van Gogh, who passed most of his much shorter life in more dire circumstances. Unlike Wright, who enjoyed decades of fame at the pinnacle of the American architectural profession, van Gogh remained practically unknown until after his death. But if they’ve encountered one another in the afterlife, they’ve certainly discussed one subject above all others: their shared appreciation for Japanese woodblock prints. Here on Open Culture, we’ve previously featured the collection of 500 such works of art that van Gogh left behind. At the end of Wright’s life in 1959, he owned about 6,000, many of which his estate had to sell to pay both Japanese art dealers and American tax collectors. We could say that Wright died as he lived, advanced age having not evidently diminished either his financial recklessness or his obsession with ukiyo‑e. The masters of that classical “art of the floating world” like Hokusai and Hiroshige were among his favorite artists of any kind. When still a teenager, Wright went to work for the architect Joseph Silsbee, who’d built a chapel for his uncle. “Silsbee’s cousin, Ernest Fenollosa, happened to be the world’s leading Western expert on Japanese art at the time,” writes Kevin Nute at The Conversation. It isn’t certain how well the young Wright knew Fenollosa — or indeed when he began collecting ukiyo‑e, writes Frank Lloyd Wright and the Art of Japan author Julia Meech-Pekarik, though he may have seen both Hokusai and Hiroshige’s works at the World’s Columbian Exposition in Chicago in 1893, “about the time he opened his practice in Oak Park.” Eight years later, “Wright made his first voyage to Japan in pursuit of prints, and he did indeed return with enough expertise to stage an exhibition of his own Hiroshige collection at the Art Institute of Chicago in March of 1906.” He returned for two months in 1913, making it clear that he was only interested in using that time to acquire more prints. cards.source_text: In some rare cases, adaptations and interpretations of a literary work can surpass the source. Despite hundreds of valiant efforts on the part of fans, filmmakers, game/toy designers, and radio producers, this has never been true of the fully-realized fantasy world in J.R.R. Tolkien’s The Hobbit and The Lord of the Rings trilogy (not that it’s ever been anyone’s intent). As we noted in a previous post, Tolkien’s fictional world is so intricate, its sources so vast and varied, that Corey Olsen, “The Tolkien Professor,” has made it his entire life’s work to open that world up to students and curious readers, such as with his eight-part lecture series on The Hobbit. One might also add illustrators to the list of Tolkien interpreters above who have—in the almost ninety years since The Hobbit’s publication and more than seventy years since the first appearance of The Lord of the Rings trilogy—done their best to visualize Tolkien’s world. But perhaps no one did so better than the master himself. Long known as a visual artist as well as a literary one, Tolkien left behind over 100 illustrations for The Hobbit, one of which adorns 2011’s HarperCollins 75th anniversary edition of the book. He also created these original cover designs for each book in The Lord of the Rings trilogy. In the long and complex publication history of Tolkien’s most famous of works, it’s unclear if these designs ever made it onto books published during his lifetime, but the sigil in the center of The Fellowship of the Ring design (above), with its ominous eye of Sauron surrounded by elvish runes and topped by the one ring, did grace the elegant, minimalist covers of the first edition of the trilogy. Tolkien’s artwork received a thorough treatment in a 1995 monograph J.R.R. Tolkien Artist & Illustrator, which covers over 60 years of Tolkien’s life as an artist, and the magic of flickr brings us this compendium of Tolkien illustrations. cards.source_text: It doesn’t quite ring true to call David Bowie a rock star. Ziggy Stardust, the neon synthetic-clad alien alter ego he both created and retired in the early seventies, was, of course, rock stardom outlandishly personified. But then, that was the concept of what turned out to be just one of many personae he deliberately crafted throughout the course of his career. That career was in music, primarily, but looking back on it today, more than a decade after Bowie’s death, it looks more like his medium was culture itself. That’s underscored by his interviews, clips from a variety of which appear in the new video above from YouTube channel T&H Inspiration. Most of T&H’s most popular videos add visuals to speeches by the popularizer of Eastern philosophy Alan Watts, who’s been featured here on Open Culture before. He and Bowie had more in common than it may seem at first, beginning with an Englishness that remained thoroughgoing no matter how far out they ventured into the world. Though Watts’ interest in Buddhism hardly needs stating, it’s worth remembering that he chose to be ordained as an Episcopalian priest rather than as a Buddhist monk. The young Bowie, for his part, very nearly took the latter path, studying under the late Lama Chime Rinpoche, who eventually told him he’d be better off going into the music business. Bowie did so, of course, but with a new “sense of transience and change, which actually became fundamental to my life and my approach to it,” as he put it decades later. That sense manifests even in his early work, but embracing and even pursuing impermanence — the impermanence of sounds, of fashions, of hit records, of life itself — also kept him from getting mired in the irrelevance or auto-kitsch that threatens every superstar. Given the belief that nothing lasts forever, “looking for the source of one’s own being becomes much more important,” as does attempting artistic or intellectual challenges at the very edge of one’s abilities. Alan Watts would probably have agreed. The bigger question is, did he ever hear “Changes”? cards.source_text: ‘The land had its own stories.’ A common narrative among European settlers was that the lands they occupied were empty and, therefore, free to claim. This assumption, imposed across many colonies, severed Indigenous peoples from places to which they held deep cultural and spiritual ties. Central Australia was no exception: the doctrine of ‘terra nullius’, used to justify British claims over Australia, treated the land as if it belonged to no one, disregarding the long histories of Aboriginal communities who had been living there for tens of thousands of years. For this short documentary, the British artist Patrick Waterhouse collaborated with the Warlukurlangu art centre to revisit that history by intervening in official colonial documents and maps. Working for several years with Warlpiri artists from Yuendumu and Nyirripi, he invited them to respond to these archival materials through their own visual languages. The film captures the collaborative process, the conversations prompted by these documents and the striking works that emerge: pieces in which colonial cartography intersects with Indigenous knowledge and art.

Over decades of research as a historian of medicine and of human bodies, I’d never imagined such a niche question. And then it was sparked in an instant, between one second and the next, in the time it takes to open a manila folder. For another project altogether I was in the UK to research the papers of Charlotte Wolff, a physician trained in Berlin in the 1920s and living in London in the late 1930s, a Jewish refugee. Opening a file labelled ‘Zoo, 1938’, I came across a massive, delicate palm print: it belonged to Mok, a lowland gorilla at London Zoo. Two days after Mok’s death, the keeper had granted Wolff special permission to enter the morgue and collect a pattern that had been too dangerous to acquire in life. Mok’s palm print was both forceful and touching. Indeed, I was tempted to literally touch, to hold hands across time, across species, and across the worlds of the living and the dead. The emotive power was unmistakeable, yet for all my training as a historian, it was inscrutable to me. I was also puzzled why Wolff, an exceptionally clever physician, seemed to be practising palm-reading, which today is associated with magic and the occult. Could there be such a thing as medical palmistry? Over time, I learned that the answer is a clear, but unlikely, ‘yes’. Wolff was looking for the so-called ‘simian line’, a particular crease that some humans share with other primate species. Long ago, in embryonic time, the patterns on each of our tiny, clenched palms were formed. For most of us, three main lines were created. For some of us – up to 5 per cent – the so-called head and heart lines fused into a single crease stretching across the palm from one side to the other. Robert De Niro, Hillary Clinton and Benedict Cumberbatch each boast a simian line on their palms. Tony Blair apparently does on both hands, an even rarer distinction. In the 1920s, the London physician Francis Crookshank delighted in announcing that even the Virgin Mary had a simian line, directing people to see for themselves in Renaissance devotional art. When Rigg learned that not only was Macnee paid significantly more than she was, but the camera operator was too, she demanded a raise. She got it, but that didn’t stop the press from labelling her as a grasping diva. Fifty years later, she told Newsnight: “Equal pay. That’s what feminism means to me, only that.” On the stage and screen, Rigg specialised in fierce, complicated women: Medea, Phèdre, Mother Courage, the wimple-clad Olenna Tyrell in Game of Thrones. When teaming with Dilla, Busta never got any volatile, flamboyant, shout-rap singles with music videos made of Tex Avery-styled antics and critical levels of fish-eye lens; never any hip-hop radio chokeholds or sneaky pop radio Trojan horses. However, the juxtaposition of Busta’s fire-breathing flow and Dilla’s muted, ill-proportioned pockets always served as a perfect chaser to the rapper’s more ostentatious moments of woo-hah and rowr-rowr and cha-cha-cha-cha-cha. Between 1996 and his death a decade later, Dilla quietly contributed seasick tracks to six of Busta’s first seven albums—a legacy of incredibly funky songs that were never marketed in a way to warrant a blue text hyperlink on Wikipedia. In November 2007, under the aegis of mixtape DJ Mick Boogie and with the blessing of Dilla’s mom, Maureen “Ma Dukes” Yancey, the Dilla-Busta Accord continued with Dillagence, featuring more unheard and underheard recordings of the rapper-producer team. It was an incredible showcase of their working relationship, with Busta often mirroring Dilla’s off-kilter rhythms and skipping melodies, dipping into Nice & Smooth flows (“Step Up”) and eating up the occasional Donut (“Best That Ever Did It”). Over the past 14 years and change, the artist known in government records as Michael Quattlebaum Jr. has been performing under a genderbending persona both braggadocious and tender. Speedrunning through genres (and artistic mediums; he recently got his MFA in Switzerland), Blanco doesn’t lay claim to any one particular sound: His songs run the gamut from industrial rap to Nine Inch Nails-style rock to ballroom. One thing Blanco has never been, though, is coy: I mean, his debut album came out swinging with the image of “white powder in both holes.” His new album, Cafe Paradiso, is still rife with sex, drugs, and rock ’n’ roll. But there’s an inward shift; while Blanco’s lyrics are as swaggering and bawdy as ever, Paradiso sounds more sensual than sensory, more relishing than confrontational. Drawing on influences from Saint Etienne to Deee-Lite’s Towa Tei, Blanco swerves head-on into slick ’80s grooves and garage rock with self-assuredness. No score yet, be the first to add. The album kicks off with disco-ball gleam. The relatively downtempo “Little Feet” is a delightful opening feint towards slow-jam chillness; never have backshots sounded more romantic. Then the album revs into gear: On “NYC DOGS,” Blanco growls and keens over buzzing, blown-out bass and B-52s-esque percussion as he urges the audience to stick out our tongues, dirty dogs that we are, and “spread like butter for me.” Listening to the standout “Butt Sex”—a sort of freaked-out, tweaked-out “Ice Cream” by New Young Pony Club—one can practically imagine Blanco strutting around stage in an undone tux with Elvis Derangement Syndrome. It’s completely unserious until you feel just how severe that bassline is. “Uglies, please exit the floor,” Blanco sneers; “Y’all don’t even get five seconds.” You almost feel for them. items.title: Fewer and Fewer Students Earn Degrees in the Humanities
items.summary: 20 years ago, nearly 15% of the undergraduate degrees conferred in the United States were in the humanities. As of 2025, that percentage is down to 8.1%. These figures are from a recent report by Humanities Indicators, a project of the American Academy of Arts & Sciences. Here are the numbers: In 2025, the nation’s colleges and universities awarded 164,847 bachelor’s degrees in the humanities—the smallest number of degrees awarded since 1991 and 30.4% below the recent high-water mark in 2012… That decline includes a particularly sharp drop of 12.7% from 2021 to 2023, followed by a more modest drop of 2.1% from 2023 to 2024, and a further decline of just 0.4% from 2024 to 2025—the smallest year-on-year decline since 2012. And most disciplines within the humanities have shown a decline: Within the humanities, almost every discipline awarded fewer degrees in 2025 than 13 years earlier… The largest proportional drops in degrees awarded occurred in religious studies (down 56.3%), area studies (53.2%), languages and literatures other than English (50.8%), English (43.8%), history (40.6%), classical studies (39.4%), and comparative literature (31%). Only three disciplines showed increases—folklore (where the small number of degrees awarded makes the numbers highly volatile), the study of the arts (with a modest 2.1% increase since 2012), and interdisciplinary humanities disciplines (where the increase was largely due to the addition of a substantial number of new programs, such as digital humanities, in the Department of Education’s 2020 revision of its Classification of Instructional Programs). How’s philosophy doing? Well, after a slight decrease last year, there has been a slight increase: In 2024, 5,763 students earned philosophy BAs. In 2025, that number was 5,918. The full report from Humanities Indicators is here. The post Fewer and Fewer Students Earn Degrees in the Humanities first appeared on Daily Nous .

items.title: Placement & AOS
items.summary: Which areas of specialization have been correlated with higher placement into “permanent” (typically tenure-track or tenured) positions over the past few years? “The broad finding is that those in Value Theory and History & Traditions (n=1125) have a higher proportion in permanent academic placement… than those in LEMM or Science, Logic, & Math (n=864),” according to Carolyn Dicey Jennings (UC Merced), who analyzed data gathered by Academic Philosophy Data and Analysis (APDA) on graduates from 2021 through 2026 and shared the results in a post at the APDA Blog. Jennings breaks down the areas of specialization into “big” (more than 100 graduates over the past five years), “mid-sized” (between 20 and 100 graduates), and “small” (fewer than 20 graduates). items.title: What Should My Children Do? by Daniel Susskind review – the case for embracing tech in the classroom
items.summary: A refreshingly optimistic book that asks us to grasp the educational opportunities of AI, rather than shrink from them In 1979, the government asked Wilfred Cockcroft, a now largely forgotten maths lecturer from the University of Hull, to write a report about a crisis in the teaching of his subject to children. It was wide-ranging and meticulous, and included a chapter on a technological innovation that was suddenly becoming available to the average consumer: the calculator. Many parents and teachers feared that the gadget would undermine a basic skill and a pillar of education – one of the sacred three Rs – producing generations of dumbed-down drones who could reach for a device in their pockets to avoid the hard graft of arithmetic. items.title: All About My Mother by Rachael Stirling review – a joyous love letter to Diana Rigg
items.summary: Beautifully written by her daughter, this is a funny and intimate eulogy to the 60s star of The Avengers who went on to specialise in fierce, complicated women The late actor Diana Rigg declined to call herself a feminist, noting: “Why would I burn my bra? I need my bra.” Nonetheless, her ideas on womanhood were ahead of their time. In an interview with Michael Parkinson, she observed how marriage was “all rather pagan, don’t you think? … A lot of women see it as security. Well, I’m not a woman who yearns for security.” Taking over from Honor Blackman as the high-kicking Emma Peel in the 1960s spy series The Avengers, Rigg refused to play subordinate sidekick to Patrick Macnee’s Steed, turning her character into a beacon of female empowerment. When Rigg learned that not only was Macnee paid significantly more than she was, but the camera operator was too, she demanded a raise. She got it, but that didn’t stop the press from labelling her as a grasping diva. Fifty years later, she told Newsnight: “Equal pay. That’s what feminism means to me, only that.” Continue reading...

items.title: Can an entire Arctic ecosystem evolve to adapt to the climate crisis?
items.summary: In the first project of its kind, scientists are trying to answer if the future of Alaska’s streams and tundra may depend not on survival of the fittest but on how species adapt together On Alaska’s North Slope, scientists tread carefully across clumps of tussock grasses toward a fast-flowing stream draining the imposing Brooks Range of ice and snow. Near Galbraith Creek, they string out a mist net for white-crowned sparrows. The birds have recently arrived from southerly latitudes, intent on feasting on the insects that will soon descend on the tundra like storm clouds. The Arctic summer is short-lived, and sparrows have only a few weeks to establish territories, find mates, lay eggs and raise their chicks on a steady diet of bugs. From every ensnared bird, the scientists collect blood, feather and faecal samples to see what they are eating and how that changes over the summer. items.title: Birdwatch: the avian equivalent of a catwalk model, blue cranes are under threat
items.summary: Numbers of the exquisitely graceful species are falling amid loss of food supply and habitat Few birds are quite as elegant as the blue crane. As I watched a pair feeding alongside a busy road in South Africa, against the rather incongruous backdrop of a herd of cows, I was struck by their sheer beauty. With a slender body, curved neck, long legs, elongated tail plumes and a subtle, dove-grey plumage, this bird really is the avian equivalent of a catwalk model. But not all is well for the blue crane. It has the smallest global range of any of the world’s 15 crane species: apart from an isolated population in Namibia, almost all are found in South Africa, where it is celebrated as the national bird. items.title: Save our seabirds from the huge windfarm due to be built near Bass Rock | Letter
items.summary: The offshore windfarm at Berwick Bank is predicted to kill more than 4,000 birds in its first year alone – among them gannets, puffins and kittiwakes, writes Ashley Davies Lev Parikian paints a vivid picture of the gannets of the Bass Rock and the impact that avian flu has had on their numbers ( Country diary, 31 August ). There’s another threat, though, and it’s one that puts some supporters of renewable energy like me in a novel situation: protesting against the construction of a windfarm. Berwick Bank will be one of the biggest offshore windfarms in the world – a few kilometres from the Bass. This is perilously close, and the RSPB has calculated that it will kill more than 4,000 seabirds in its first year alone, among them gannets, puffins and endangered kittiwakes. Continue reading...
